name: The Negativity Bias
statement: Bad events, emotions, and news hit us harder than equally strong good ones.
meaning: The negativity bias is the tendency for negative events, emotions, and information to affect us more strongly than neutral or positive things of equal intensity. A harsh word outweighs a kind one, a loss stings more than an equal gain pleases, and bad news grips us more than good. Summed up as bad is stronger than good, it describes a systematic asymmetry in how the mind weights the negative.
mechanism: An evolutionary account holds that threats are more urgent than opportunities: an organism that heavily weights dangers is more likely to survive, so negatives recruit greater attention, memory, and effort to minimise their consequences. This shows up as longer looking at negative images, better recall of negative information, and steeper learning from punishment. Analyses distinguish several facets: negatives loom larger at equal magnitude, intensify faster as they draw near, dominate mixed positive-and-negative wholes, and are conceptualised in richer, more differentiated ways.

examples.text: A single piece of harsh feedback tends to weigh more heavily and linger longer than several compliments of equal force.
Negative traits are treated as more diagnostic of character, so a bad first impression is held with more confidence and is harder to overturn.
Bad news draws more attention and coverage than good news, reflecting and feeding the negativity bias at the scale of media.

variants.name: The four facets
variants.text: Rozin and Royzman's analysis into negative potency, a steeper negative gradient, negativity dominance in mixed wholes, and greater negative differentiation.

variants.name: Positivity offsets
variants.text: Domains and life stages, such as a shift toward positivity in older adults, where the negative does not dominate, showing the bias is not universal across the lifespan.

whyItMatters: Its reach across relationships, decision-making, media, marketing, well-being, and politics is so broad that its authors described it as approaching a general principle of psychology. It explains why negative events shape us disproportionately, why bad feedback and bad news carry outsized weight, and it informs how we might counter that tilt, from cultivating positive experiences to reading the news with a corrective eye.

working.text: recognise that negatives register more strongly, and consciously give due weight to positive information and feedback.
anticipate that a single bad event or remark will loom larger than an equal good one, in yourself and others.
in relationships and communication, offset the disproportionate weight of the negative with more, and more salient, positives.

limits: It is well supported and cross-domain, but the size of the asymmetry is context-dependent and it is not universal: positivity offsets exist in some domains, and negativity bias emerges only in the second half of the first year of life and can shift toward positivity in older adults. Its link to loss aversion is real but not clean, since the monetary case is not a tidy demonstration. Popular fixed ratios of how much more negatives count are folk quantifications, not established constants.
misreadings: Bad is stronger than good does not mean people are net pessimists or that positive information is ignored; it means negatives carry disproportionate weight at equal intensity. It is not identical to loss aversion, which is a specific decision-theoretic case that the monetary evidence does not cleanly support. And it is not uniform across the lifespan, being absent in early infancy and softened in older age.
origin: Reviewed and named in two influential 2001 papers, Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer, and Vohs's 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good' and Rozin and Royzman's analysis of negativity dominance and contagion.

sources.text: Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," Review of General Psychology 5 (2001): 323-370. — the cross-domain review of the asymmetry.
Negativity bias, Wikipedia. — the greater weight of the negative, the four facets, and the lifespan and loss-aversion caveats.
